issues.item: Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Unfamiliar Places' is an avoidance/safety behaviour rather than a threat appraisal item. In this profile, the Threat node otherwise contains felt current danger and reliving; this item is misclassified and weakens within-node coherence.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Authority Figures' is not phrased as a strategy and appears to describe a trigger category. It is also weakly supported by the rest of the profile, since no memory, threat, or appraisal content specifically involves authorities or uniforms. This creates a cross-node mismatch and a node-level inconsistency within Maladaptive Strategies.

vignette:
Fatima is a 55-year-old divorced woman of Middle Eastern origin who has been living in the United States for nearly a decade, working as an HVAC technician for a commercial maintenance company in the Houston area. She came to the clinic after her supervisor placed her on a performance improvement plan, noting that she had become increasingly unreliable - arriving late to job sites, refusing certain assignments without explanation, and appearing visibly distressed during routine inspections of large industrial facilities. Her PCL-5 score of 63 places her presentation in the severe range, and what emerged across the first several sessions was a clinical picture deeply rooted in the experience of forced displacement.

Fatima fled her home country during a period of sustained civil conflict. The crossing that broke something in her happened at night, on a overcrowded inflatable vessel crossing a wide stretch of open water. At some point the boat began to take on water, and in the chaos that followed - people screaming, the vessel listing, the cold seeping through clothing - she found herself clinging to the wet, rough rubber of the deflating hull, certain she was going to drown. She did not drown. Others did not survive. The silence that fell over the water after the worst of it passed was, she has said, more terrifying than the noise. She reached the far shore. She has never spoken about what she saw in the water.

In the years since, certain things have become unbearable without her fully understanding why. Water is the most obvious: driving over bridges in Houston, passing the bayous that flood seasonally, even seeing a news segment about coastal storms can pull the memory back with a force that feels less like remembering and more like returning. When a trigger lands - the sight of flooding, or the particular rough texture of certain industrial rubber gaskets she handles on the job - the memory does not arrive as a narrative. It arrives as sensation: cold, weight, the smell of salt and diesel. The memory, when it returns, carries with it such an overwhelming wave of emotion that Fatima has learned she must put down whatever she is holding and leave the room. She has described the recollections as so extreme that part of her still cannot accept they happened to her - that the woman clinging to that hull was herself. Alongside the disbelief comes shame, a conviction that she should have done something differently, that she should have been stronger, that she did not do enough for the people around her. The shame makes her reluctant to let the memory surface fully, and so it remains fragmented, unprocessed, and potent.

What the memory produces, when it does surface, is a state of acute threat that then feeds back into the memory itself, amplifying it. Fatima has come to feel that unusual silence - the kind that settles over a large mechanical room when equipment shuts down unexpectedly - signals imminent danger, the same way the silence on the water did. In that heightened state, she finds herself scanning every room she enters, noting exits, calculating distances. The scanning is not voluntary; it is continuous and exhausting. She experiences intrusive flashbacks in which she is not in an HVAC plant in Houston but back on the water, and these episodes leave her shaking and ashamed.

Over time, Fatima developed a set of strategies that she believed kept her safe but that have tightened the trap considerably. She now plans an escape route before entering any enclosed space - a habit that, at work, means she spends the first minutes of every job site visit mentally mapping exits rather than attending to the task. This constant preparation keeps threat at the front of her awareness, which in turn makes her more reactive to the textures and environmental cues she encounters on the job. The rumination about those she blames for the conditions that forced her flight - the officials, the smugglers - occupies her during the long drives between sites, and that dwelling brings the memory closer to the surface, making the next trigger more potent. Each strategy intended to create safety instead keeps her perceptually primed, the loop tightening week by week.

What finally brought Fatima to the clinic was not the performance plan alone. It was a morning when she encountered a flooded parking lot at a job site, turned her van around, drove home, and did not call in. She sat in her apartment for two days. She is most afraid, she says, that she will lose her job - the one thing, she believes, that still gives her structure and dignity. What she hopes for, more quietly, is to stop feeling like the water is always just beneath her feet.
